newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.N. still not satisfied with Iraqi disarmament.
newsitem.headline: U.N. still not satisfied with Iraqi disarmament.

text.p: The discovery in Iraq of four wrecked missile engines has not satisfied the United Nations that Iraq has destroyed all of its banned rockets, a U.N. arms official in Baghdad said on Tuesday.
"They (the engines) may close some of the gap but will not resolve all our concerns," Roger Knight, assistant director of Baghdad's Ongoing Monitoring and Verification (OMV) centre, told Reuters.

A U.N. ballistic missile team spent three weeks in Baghdad this month supervising Iraqi digs of sites where the Iraqis said they had unilaterally destroyed and buried a large number of their long-range missiles.
Knight said the team of 10 experts under Frenchman Michael Bordin left Baghdad on January 25.
Under terms that ended the 1991 Gulf War over Kuwait, Iraq is obliged to destroy missiles with ranges greater than 150 km (93 miles).

The U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) overseeing destruction of all such Iraqi missiles in addition to its nuclear, biological and chemical arms says it still suspects that Iraq has not yet come clean on its banned rockets.
Knight said Iraqis used bulldozers and other earth-moving equipment in latest digs for missile parts. "Four engines and other components were unearthed," he said.

He said the excavations, the first on such a large-scale in search of banned weapons, were carried out as part of an Iraqi initiative to try to substantiate claims that all its banned missiles were destroyed.
Knight said the significance of the Iraqi discovery would only be determined after "thorough analysis" by international experts.

Iraq and UNSCOM are at odds over how and where to analyse more than 100 missile parts salvaged from other sites close to Baghdad. About 80 of them are packed in boxes for shipment abroad and the rest plus the latest four engines are stored in warehouses under strict U.N. surveillance.
UNSCOM insists on having them analysed in the United States. Iraq would like them to be shipped to either Russia or France.

Knight said UNSCOM chairman Rolf Ekeus would visit Baghdad by mid-February in the latest bid to defuse the standoff. He said apart from differences on missiles, the two sides still needed to clear up issues in other weapons areas, particularly the chemical and biological spheres.
The government newspaper al-Jumhouriya last week said Iraq was determined to close its weapons files to have the ban on its oil exports completely lifted.
The U.N. permitted Iraq to resume partial oil sales in December to help it alleviate the effect of sanctions still in place for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The removal of restrictions on Iraq's oil exports depends to a large extent on a clean bill of health from UNSCOM that all its weapons of mass destruction are either annihilated or rendered harmless.
